newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka forces strike Tamil rebels after lull.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka forces strike Tamil rebels after lull.

text.p: Sri Lanka's military, using tanks, artillery and air strikes, launched a fresh strike on the heartland of Tamil Tiger rebel territory on Sunday after a lull of more than a month, military officials said.
It was the first major push for more than a month by security forces, who had dug in north of the rebel-held northern town of Kilinochchi, a gateway to the rebels' jungle stronghold of Wanni.

The separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), who seek an independent homeland for minority Tamils in the island's north and east, earlier this year lost their stronghold of the Jaffna peninsula which they had ruled for almost a decade with their own administration, courts and police.
"The military operation started this morning and the attack continued throughout the day," a military officer told Reuters.
The army, flanked by tanks and artillery, advanced from the northern juncture town of Paranthan towards Kilinochchi.
Air force bombers and helicopter gunships also pounded rebel positions to assist the army's push but the rebels fought back strongly, the officer said, asking not to be identified.
"There was fair amount of resistance from the LTTE," he said. "Eleven soldiers have been killed in the operation. The LTTE must have suffered heavy casualties because of air and artillery strikes."
The officer said several soldiers were also injured, including a lieutenant colonel in the Armoured Corp.

An LTTE radio broadcast confirmed heavy shelling by the military and said several homes in Kilinochchi were damaged. It said civilians living in the outskirts of the town began fleeing the area because of the shelling.
A Red Cross official who came to the army-held town of Vavuniya, 70 km (44 miles) south of Kilinochchi, from the rebel-controlled area said he heard heavy bombing and saw military planes flying.
The military balance has remained largely unchanged since the LTTE handed the military its worst setback in the 13-year war in July when they overran a strategic army base.
The army launched an offensive soon after the LTTE wiped out the northeastern Mullaitivu camp, killing or capturing almost its entire garrison of 1,400 men.
But the army's push, advancing south from the northern Jaffna peninsula, had been stalled near Kilinochchi.
Diplomats said there had been a lull in the war recently partly because the army had exhausted itself after a thrust towards Kilinochchi in July.
"About 30 percent of the military's full strength has been kept in Jaffna since its recapture of the peninsula last April," an Asian diplomat said. The total army strength is 100,000.
Neelan Tiruchelvam, fellow at the International Centre for Ethinic Studies and a member of parliament, said he saw no end in the near future to the stalemate in the ethnic war.

"I don't see any breakthrough in the military operation. Unfortunately war has its own dynamics. Each party to a war wants to tilt the military balance in their favour. So it is an unending cycle," he said.

Tiruchelvam said a political solution was the only way to end the conflict, but diplomats said bickering by the ruling and opposition parties appeared set to scuttle a peace package proposed by President Chandrika Kumaratunga last year.
The package, offering to devolve wide-ranging powers to minority Tamils through a constitutional revision, aims to end the war which the government says has killed more than 50,000 people.
